title: Intervals
summary: Merge overlapping intervals after sorting by start, insert into a sorted list in one pass, find the busiest moment with a sweep line, and remove the fewest.
intro: An interval is a stretch with a start and an end: a meeting, a booking, a range of pages. Most interval problems begin with a sort, which puts the intervals that can overlap next to each other. This lesson merges overlaps, inserts into a sorted list in one pass, finds the busiest moment with a sweep line, and removes the fewest intervals so the rest fit. The programs store an interval as `type Interval struct{ Start, End int }`. A `[2]int` works the same way, with `iv[0]` and `iv[1]` in place of the fields.

steps.title: Merging overlapping intervals

example.title: Closed stretches of road
example.prompt: Read roadwork zones as kilometer ranges, merge the ones that overlap or touch, and print each closed stretch and how many there are.
example.output:
km 1 to 2
km 3 to 8
km 12 to 20
km 25 to 27
closed stretches: 4
example.explanation: After the sort the zones run 1 to 2, 3 to 5, 5 to 8, 12 to 15, 14 to 20, 16 to 18, and 25 to 27. 3 to 5 starts after 2, so it opens a new stretch. 5 to 8 starts exactly where 3 to 5 ends, and `<=` joins them into 3 to 8. 14 to 20 starts inside 12 to 15 and pushes the end to 20, while 16 to 18 lies inside and leaves it at 20. Once the zones are sorted, the walk looks at each one once.

practice.title: Watched parts of a video
practice.prompt:
A video player logs the parts of a video someone played, in seconds, in any order and with repeats. Merge them and add up the time watched.

1. The starter reads `n` parts into `parts`.
2. Add `"sort"` to the imports and sort `parts` by start.
3. Merge the parts that overlap or touch into `merged`, keeping the bigger end.
4. The starter prints each merged part as `start-end`, then `watched: T seconds`, where T adds up `End - Start` over the merged parts.

Input:

```text
5
40 55
0 10
50 70
10 15
58 60
```

Expected output:

```text
0-15
40-70
watched: 45 seconds
```
hints: Sort with `sort.Slice(parts, func(i, j int) bool { return parts[i].Start < parts[j].Start })`.
Set `last := len(merged) - 1` for each part, and check `last >= 0` before you read `merged[last]`, so the first part starts a block.
Grow the block only when the part ends later. A part inside it, like 58 to 60 inside 50 to 70, must not shrink it.

steps.title: Inserting into a sorted list

example.title: Joining highlights
example.prompt: Read a document's highlighted character ranges, sorted and not overlapping, and one new highlight. Join the new one with every highlight it overlaps or touches, and print the highlights after.
example.explanation: 2 to 5 ends before 12, so the first loop copies it. 9 to 12 ends exactly where the new highlight starts, so `End < add.Start` is false and the second loop takes it: the highlight now starts at 9. 15 to 18 starts exactly where it ends, and `Start <= add.End` joins that one too, so the highlight grows to 9 to 18. 25 starts after 18, so the loop stops and the last append copies 25 to 30. `add` is a copy of `h`, so growing it inside `insert` leaves `h` as it was.

practice.title: Downloaded chunks
practice.prompt:
A download keeps the byte ranges it already has, sorted and not overlapping. Chunks arrive one at a time, and each one joins the ranges it overlaps or touches.

1. The starter reads `n` ranges, which can be 0, then `q` chunks. It inserts each chunk and prints the ranges after it, one line per chunk.
2. Finish `insert` in one pass: copy the ranges that end before `add` starts, grow `add` over the ranges it overlaps, then append `add` and the rest.

Input:

```text
2
0 20
50 70
3
30 40
40 50
10 35
```

Expected output:

```text
0-20 30-40 50-70
0-20 30-70
0-70
```
hints: Use the example's two loops with one index `i`: the first runs while `ranges[i].End < add.Start`, the second while `ranges[i].Start <= add.End`.
In the second loop take the smaller start and the bigger end, so a chunk inside a range, like 12 to 15 inside 10 to 20, grows to cover it.
Finish with `out = append(out, add)` and `return append(out, ranges[i:]...)`. With no ranges at all, both loops skip and the result is just `add`.

steps.title: A sweep line for the busiest moment

example.title: Busiest hour in a garage
example.prompt: Read when each car arrived and left, and print the most cars in the garage at once and the first hour that happened. A car that leaves at an hour frees its space before a car that arrives at that hour takes it.
example.output: most cars at once: 2, first at hour 9
example.explanation: The count reaches 2 at hour 9. At hour 11 one car leaves and another arrives, and since the leaving event sorts first, the count drops to 1 before it climbs back to 2. Hour 12 works the same way. With the arrivals first, the count would touch 3 at hour 11, though only two cars were ever there together. `count > best` keeps the first hour the count reached 2, not a later one that only ties it.

practice.title: Peak load on a bus
practice.prompt:
Groups of people ride a bus. Each group gets on at one stop and off at a later one. Find the most people on board at once.

1. The starter reads `n` groups as `on off people`, with at least 1 person in each group.
2. Add two events per group: `+people` at stop `on` and `-people` at stop `off`.
3. Add `"sort"` to the imports. Sort the events by stop, with the people getting off before the people getting on at the same stop.
4. Walk the events with a running count, keeping the peak and the first stop that reached it. The starter prints `peak: P people at stop S`.

Input:

```text
4
1 5 10
2 4 6
4 8 7
6 9 3
```

Expected output:

```text
peak: 17 people at stop 4
```
hints: Add both events at once: `events = append(events, Event{on, people}, Event{off, -people})`.
Sort like the example: compare `Stop` first, and on a tie put the smaller `Delta` first. Getting off is negative, so it comes before getting on.
Use `count > peak`, so a later stop that only ties the peak doesn't replace the first one.

steps.title: Removing the fewest to end overlaps

example.title: One tennis court
example.prompt: Read court bookings that may clash, keep the most that fit on one court, and print the ones kept and how many to cancel. A booking can start right when another ends.
example.output:
keep 9 to 11
keep 11 to 13
keep 13 to 14
cancel 3
example.explanation: Sorted by end, the bookings are 9 to 11, 10 to 12, 11 to 13, 13 to 14, 8 to 15, and 12 to 16. 9 to 11 ends first, so it's kept. 10 to 12 starts before 11 and is skipped. 11 to 13 starts exactly at 11, and `>=` keeps it, then 13 to 14 fits the same way. 8 to 15 and 12 to 16 start before 14, so they're cancelled. Sorted by start, 8 to 15 would come first and block every other booking. This example keeps the bookings themselves in `kept`, so the last end is `kept[len(kept)-1].End`.

practice.title: Festival screenings
practice.prompt:
A film festival lists screenings as `start end` in minutes, in any order, and the same screening can be listed more than once. You can't watch two at once, but you can walk out of one and into another that starts that minute. Watch as many as you can.

1. The starter reads `n` screenings into `shows`.
2. Add `"sort"` to the imports and sort `shows` by end.
3. Count in `watch` each screening that starts at or after the end of the last one you kept.
4. The starter prints `watch W, skip S`, where S is the number you skip.

Input:

```text
5
0 240
15 105
135 225
105 135
230 260
```

Expected output:

```text
watch 4, skip 1
```
hints: Sort with `sort.Slice(shows, func(i, j int) bool { return shows[i].End < shows[j].End })`.
Keep `lastEnd`, the end of the last screening you kept. A screening fits when `watch == 0 || s.Start >= lastEnd`.
Sorting by start fails here: 0 to 240 starts first, and keeping it blocks every other screening.

recap:
- Sort by start with `sort.Slice`, and any overlap is with the block you're building. Grow `merged[last].End` or append a new block.
- `<=` merges intervals that only touch, and `<` keeps them apart. Keep the bigger end, so an interval inside a block can't shrink it.
- Change a slice element through its index. A copy of the struct changes only the copy.
- To insert into a sorted list with no overlaps, copy the ones that end before it starts, grow the new one over the ones it overlaps, then append it and the rest. That's O(n) with no sort.
- A sweep line turns each interval into a +1 and a -1 event, sorts them by time, and keeps a running count. On a tie, ends go first when touching intervals don't overlap.
- To remove the fewest, sort by end and keep each interval that starts at or after the last kept end. The rest are the removals.
- Sorting costs O(n log n), and every walk after it is O(n).
